title: Given an array that may contain duplicate integers, return all unique permutations.
shortTitle: Permutations II (with duplicates) — sort then skip same-level duplicates

s1_definition.profdef: Sort the array, then run permutation backtracking with a used[] array and an extra guard: skip nums[i] if it equals nums[i-1] and the previous equal element has not been used at this branch (used[i-1] is false). This canonical ordering ensures each group of identical values is placed left-to-right, generating each distinct permutation exactly once.
s1_definition.analogy: National Bank of India schedules batches where some are interchangeable (same type). Swapping two identical batches does not create a genuinely different schedule. By insisting identical batches are always placed in their fixed left-to-right order, you count each truly distinct schedule once.
s1_definition.oneliner: Sort, then skip a duplicate value whose equal predecessor is unused at this branch to avoid repeated permutations.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Sort the array, then run permutation backtracking with a used[] array and an extra guard: skip nums[i] if it equals nums[i-1] and the previous equal element has not been used at this branch (used[i-1] is false). This canonical ordering ensures each group of identical values is placed left-to-right, generating each distinct permutation exactly once.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** National Bank of India schedules batches where some are interchangeable (same type). Swapping two identical batches does not create a genuinely different schedule. By insisting identical batches are always placed in their fixed left-to-right order, you count each truly distinct schedule once.

**One line to remember:** Sort, then skip a duplicate value whose equal predecessor is unused at this branch to avoid repeated permutations.

sections.s2_technical:
After sorting, inside the loop skip used elements as before, and additionally skip when the current equals the previous and the previous is not currently used. For example: `if (used[i] || (i>0 && nums[i]==nums[i-1] && !used[i-1])) continue;`.

The `!used[i-1]` test enforces that among equal values, an earlier copy must be placed before a later copy, which removes the mirror-image duplicates. If instead you wrote `used[i-1]`, you would keep duplicates and drop valid ones, so the condition direction matters.

The worst-case time is O(n · n!) when all elements are distinct, with duplicates pruning branches. A senior nuance is that the same canonical-order trick (fix the order within equal groups) is the general recipe for de-duplicating any permutation/combination enumeration.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — At National Bank of India, a schedule is built from job slots where some jobs are of an identical type, and the planner needs every genuinely distinct schedule, not reorderings of identical jobs. This is exactly how unique permutations works.

Problem 2 — Swapping two identical jobs must not count as a new schedule. This is exactly why the array is sorted and equal values are kept in canonical order via the used-predecessor guard.

The mini-project builds a `ScheduleEnumerator`, a `BankLogFormatter`, and a runnable demo.

sections.s5_journey:
The input one, one, two is already sorted.

Step 1: Placing the first one, then the second one, then two yields [1,1,2].

Step 2: Placing the first one, then two, then the second one yields [1,2,1].

Step 3: Placing two first, then the two ones yields [2,1,1].

Step 4: Any attempt to place the second one before the first at a branch is blocked by the canonical-order guard, so no duplicate schedules appear.

Step 5: The three distinct schedules are produced once each.

```text
2026-10-27T00:00:00Z [INFO] Generated 3 distinct schedules
2026-10-27T00:00:00Z [INFO] Schedule: [1, 1, 2]
2026-10-27T00:00:00Z [INFO] Schedule: [1, 2, 1]
2026-10-27T00:00:00Z [INFO] Schedule: [2, 1, 1]
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```text
  sort [1,1,2]
  guard: skip nums[i]==nums[i-1] && !used[i-1]
    [1,1,2] [1,2,1] [2,1,1]
    (second 1 before first 1 → pruned)
  unique permutations = 3
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Permutations II generates every unique ordering when the input contains duplicate values. I sort first so equal values are adjacent, then run the standard permutation backtracking with the used array, and I add one guard: I skip the current element if it equals the previous element and that previous equal element is not currently used in this branch. That guard fixes a canonical left-to-right order within each group of identical values, which is what removes the mirror-image duplicates.

The direction of the condition matters: testing that the equal predecessor is not used forces earlier copies to be placed before later copies. If I flipped it to require the predecessor to be used, I would keep duplicates and drop valid permutations. The worst-case cost is still O(n times n factorial), reduced in practice as duplicates prune branches.

In my project at National Bank of India, a planner built schedules from job slots where several jobs were of an identical type, and it needed every genuinely distinct schedule rather than reshuffles of interchangeable jobs. This sorted canonical-order technique produced each distinct schedule exactly once, and it is the same general recipe I use to de-duplicate any permutation or combination enumeration.
